I tried the game because I was curious about it's story which was interesting and a lot deeper than I thought it would be. There are different ways to go through the game although there are some missions that you have to fulfill in order to progress, the side quests are also fun. In addition, the extra widgets (and mini-game) and the fact that you can change the colour of your UI are little details that make the game's fun increase.

The music is the one thing that I both liked and didn't like. While it fit the atmosphere when you're playing, it can get distracting at times (especially when a part of the mission is time-sensitive). Maybe if it was softer or you had the option to use your own tracks it would be better. There were also some bugs I encountered while playing causing me to restart the game twice. The first was an error wherein it told me thtat the mission I just completed wasn't finished and I couldn't progress through the game (as it was a main mission). The second one was a similar issue later on. A simple restart of the game fixed it and I didn't have any trouble with it afterwards.

The graphics are simple and easy on the eyes and so is the font although I wouldn't mind if it was a teensy bit bigger. 

The gameplay is simple and after a while, the commands are easy to memorize. I enjoy the puzzle aspect of the game and there are different ways to play through. One challenge (and perhaps my next playthrough) would be playing the whole game simply in terminal mode to see if (1) it's possible, (2) how fast I can do it, and (3) how challenging it is. 

Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone interested in programming whether just beginning (as it helps teach focus, critical thinking, and memorization) or already pretty in deep (cause it's fun!). It's a great game and pretty cool to play around your friends.

Wow, Hacknet is one immersive command line game.
You get to pick up the left overs of a now dead hacker, following in his footsteps, slowly taking on harder challenges and making a name for yourself.
Hacknet offers a tight narrative (which is completely text based) and enthralling 'hacking'

Pros:
 - presentation. I know a lot of people will be turned off by a CL interface game. but heck (huehue), it's beautiful, intuitive and well designed. plus you can download more UIs from servers and people you hacked
 - gameplay. it's relatively easy, requiring (so far, I'm roughly 4 hours into the game) simple management skills, a keen eye and some reading and prioritizing. the hacking is served well, not letting you button mash, but rather focused on the finer points such as: reading emails for usernames and passwords, changing websites headers into vulgarities, finding the right tools and balance, covering your tracks.
     a lot of the gameplay is indeed done over a command line interface, which, exactly, means you type out what you wanna do. there's helps, and little tools making it a lot easier than real life hacking could ever be.
- Story. it's a pretty cool mix of paranoia, technology and a weird form of justice. no one talks, no fancy cutscenes. it's all in your head, buddy
 - immersion. yeah, the computers you hack are rather empty, but what is on there is hilarious and often gives small hints to connections between the hackers you 'meet' (I think, at least
 - music. absolutely perfect. 

Cons:
 - uhm, let me think ... hmmm ... no, it is exactly what it says it is. and then some

Verdict:

You like hacking/hacking movies or just recently discovered Mr Robot or the deep web?
Well, come on in. this is a perfect supplement to your diet.
Hacknet is pretty (for CL standards :D as I work in IT I actually find it gorgeous), fun and fast paced. It will test your patience, but mostly your ability to read and type properly.
But nothing is keeping it from delivering the best hacker game since Uplink, if not even a tick better.
And it is totally worth the price tag

I was really, really impressed by this game. While incredibly old by this point, I still consider Uplink to be the pinnacle of hacking "simulation" games. While other games sometimes offered more technical depth to the hacking procedures than Uplink, they didn't manage to immerse you in the story like Uplink did. They didn't make me disconnect from the internet out of paranoia like the first time I played Uplink. And while I can't say that Hacknet made me disconnect from the internet (mostly due to knowledge and experience gained over the past 14 years), it made me fall in love with the genre all over again. 

While the basics of the game are straightforward (connecting to nodes, overloading proxies, hacking ports, erasing logs, etc...), you are rewarded for being curious. Finding helpful programs, extra information on your targets, or the hilarious IRC logs that are included from bash.org are just some of the things you can find. Some of the later levels are quite challenging despite the simple mechanics. And there is an immense sense of accomplishment when you back-hack someone who wrecked your system, only to get all of their information, hack them, and completely wipe their terminal.

There are a ton of references to all kinds of hacker related media. Movies, games (with plenty aimed at Uplink), nerd culture, prominent authors, and some well-known security groups all get nods from this game. On top of that, some of the information you gain access to while on contracts is absolutely hilarious. Sure, there are a few grammatical/spelling errors here and there, but the content of the game is still outstanding.

I highly recommend this game to anyone who played Uplink, or is a fan of computers and computer security in general. No, it's not realistic, it's not accurate, it's not perfect...but it is damn fun.

This game is very, very good. On the surface it seems like a hacking game somewhat in the style of games like Uplink, but with a huge amount of polish. However, when you actually get in to it, its better described as a really clever puzzle game with a very compelling story, wrapped in a layer of hacking. The music and the visuals are fantastic, the whole package is put together to make it feel less like you're loading up a game from steam, and more like you're logging in to a VM and stepping in to the story.

Prospective buyers need to know that this game requires you to learn and use command line functions in order to do most stuff. It does an adequate job of explaining these to the user, however if I had one criticism it would be in this area.  Had I not had command line experience in the past, I would have found the game much less accessible. I feel the game could have done a better job of introducing these concepts to a command line novice.

With that said, if you like puzzle games, if you like a good mystery, if you have any interest in hacking or computer security, and the idea of a command-line interface doesnt put you off, this game is a must buy.

As a semi-realistic hacking game, Hacknet delivers one of the most enjoyable experience available. While rich in things to do, it doesn't get overly complicated. 
The storyline doesn't prevent you from taking your time, except of course when you've breached into a well secured node and a tracer is upon you. Overall you feel like a real baddass hacking your way into the many servers available, private or corporate. I've made a second playthrough immediately after finishing the first, only because I wanted to test different approches to the multiple contracts you get. Note that some side missions won't be accessible anymore after you complete certain story missions, so if you like to be thorough, get these done first. From a gameplay perspective, it might get a bit repetitive to some players, but the music, the interface, the hidden secrets and the number of programs available make it, I feel, quite an immersive experience.

The real joy of it is that you can (almost completely, if you feel like it) play it all using only your keyboard. This wasn't possible with previous games of that genre.

If you are into 'hacking' stuff and believe you can be at ease learning some basic Unix commands, you'll certainly enjoy Hacknet!

This is the 3rd review I'm writing for this game, and honestly, when talking about this game, I am both bored and felt that it ended too soon.  The game is short, mind you.  It takes about 5 to 6 hours to complete.  Most of this time is spent fannying about, doing the games' equivilent of 'go there, kill 10 of these things', as the game frequently breaks you away from the main story/context to have you perform side missions, that usually boil down to 'hack x, delete y.'

Why am I recommending this game, saying it ended too soon?  I say this because the last two missions are two of the most cleverly crafted puzzles I've ever seen.  'Project Junebug' and 'Bit Foundation' are stellar works of glory.  I'll focus on Project Junebug, as the Bit Foundation is the final story mission (the story ends spectacularly, by the way).   Obvious spoiler alert for ahead.

The game's side missions usually work as a sort of key insert thing.   Hack 4 ports, using 4 specific commands you get earlier in the game, Port Hack, boom, in, done.  No challenge, besides when there's a tracer, but simply disconnect and reconnect, and you're good as gravy.

Project Junebug was shaping up to be another one of those things.  As I hacked the medical terminal, I thought it was clever, having to use intuition to find the IP for a heart monitor, to kill a guy.  Connecting to said IP, I found that it required access to Port 104, where up until that point I only found stuff for ports 22, 25, 28, 1433, and 88.  Not wishing to go further, it required me to hack several computers slightly hinted at, and it was brilliant, as it forced me to use inginuity and my brain to track it down.

Note to Developers:  If you made the game more like THAT, other than the slog through Entropy and CSEC, then you'd have my full support.  Say utilize the 'find and replace' skill more, or maybe give us some way to hack to second computer by using the first.  Just suggestions.

This is an amazing game. It's completely reliant on reading a lot of text, but it fits in with the hacker-working-from-their-terminal kind of narrative the story thrusts you into. The soundtrack is a perfect mix of chill techno music as well as some more faster-paced action songs that helps immerse you into all the commands you're going to be throwing at servers as you attempt to break in. What's particularly interesting is that the game uses several true linux commands for many of the common functions (ls, rm, scp) that really make it feel like a real operating system you're using to break into systems around the internet.

On the minus side, it's kind of easy to get caught up in rushing through systems without really stopping to poke around. With the threat of active security features giving a sense of urgency to complete my tasks and move on, I can't help but feel like I missed out on files I should have been reading that contacts in the game would reference after I completed objectives and progressed the story. Still, it seems like a rather authentic hacking simulator, making use of that thrilling text-based console the media associates so dearly with hacker-types, and turning it into the backbone of an enjoyable game.

If you want to learn UNIX commands go get yourself a raspberry pi, the command list they have is very short and the wildcard isn't fully flexible. While they use real terminology a lot of it is still very Holywood’s version of hacking.

If you want an entertaining and accessible game which is a decent successor to uplink with good music and a story get it.

Like uplink some of the actions get rather repetitive but thanks to an autocompleting terminal it’s not too bad.
Lots of easter eggs and the ability to hack the tutorial script, the email server which sends you missions and even the ability to delete your “computers” .sys files is rather fun.

Game will be a lot better if the dev ever implements the multiplayer he wanted.
